We can thus begin to form an idea of the vast quantity of unpublished manuscripts belonging to the Shaykhi spiritual lineage. The brief catalogue entries allow us to glimpse how, in this shaykh's writings, the spiritual philosophy grounded in the teaching of the Imams—whose foundations Shaykh Ahmad and Sayyed Kazem had already established—was extended, developed, and consolidated in every detail.

Unfortunately, virtually nothing of this work has yet become known in the West. Yet it is an essential monument of Shiite thought, and so long as we remain ignorant of it, our understanding of religious experience will lack something equally essential. We hope to devote to it the research it deserves.

There may be something arbitrary about selecting particular titles from the immense body of Mohammad Karim-Khan's writings. Nevertheless, let us mention the great Fasl al-Khitâb (II, p. 206), a systematic collection of traditions (hadîth and akhbâr), published in lithograph in Tehran in 1302 AH (1885), in a folio volume of 1,508 pages.

There is also the Tarîq al-Najât (II, p. 201), devoted to the knowledge of the spiritual path, published in lithograph in 1344 AH (1925), in a folio volume of 555 pages.

The Kitâb al-fitrat al-salîma (II, p. 193) offers a synthesis of spiritual philosophy built upon the "four pillars": the unity of God (tawhîd), prophethood (nobowwat), the Imamate (imâmat), and the Shiite community (shî'a). The author developed this synthesis further in a major Persian work entitled Irshâd al-awâmm (II, pp. 184–186), which may be translated as Spiritual Guidance for the General Community of Believers. It offers a complete and exceptionally accessible synthesis and is still read diligently by all Shaykhis. Its most recent edition was published in Kerman in 1355 AH (1936), in four parts bound as two folio volumes.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i

A collection of ten important treatises was also published in Kerman in 1354 AH (1935), in an octavo volume of 897 pages. All his scientific writings remain in manuscript: works on medicine and alchemy, and the great treatise on the color red, which more than once calls to mind Goethe's Farbenlehre, his Theory of Colours.

We cannot recall this noble figure without a quiet sadness. It is almost as if, in striking at this shaykh, his persecutors had wished to wound the Shaykhi school itself.

Born on 19 Moharram 1263 AH (1846), Hajj Mohammad-Khan (pp. 56–71) owed his intellectual and spiritual formation chiefly to his own father, Hajj Mohammad Karim-Khan. Very early on, he became his father's collaborator, and it was from their close cooperation that the enormous, systematic collection of traditions known as the Fasl al-Khitâb, mentioned above, emerged.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01402

This collaboration continued until Mohammad Karim-Khan's death. Thereafter, Mohammad-Khan in turn adopted the same method of instruction toward his younger brother, Zaynol-'Abidin-Khan, who would one day become his own successor. From an early age, the adolescent and his elder brother were intimate friends and collaborators.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01403

Once the Fasl al-Khitâb was completed, Hajj Mohammad Karim-Khan granted his son, who had thus demonstrated his abilities, a comprehensive ijâzat, authorizing him to teach and transmit the tradition. Several witnesses also confirm the spiritual authority conferred upon the son at this early age.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01404

In addition to the authorization received from his own father, by far the most important, Hajj Mohammad-Khan received a considerable number of others. Some are mentioned at the beginning of his Kitâb al-Mobîn, the largest of his works yet published. Among them were authorizations from Shaykh 'Ali Bahrani (see also §4 below), Molla Hosayn Ganjavi, and especially Shaykh Ja'far ibn Mohammad-Taqi.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01405

We have already noted that this last figure was the son of Molla Barghani himself. Through his long friendship with the Shaykhis, he seems to have wished to make amends for his father's misconduct toward Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01406

As his writings attest, Mohammad-Khan Kermani's life was essentially that of a scholar and a man of spiritual devotion, wholly absorbed in research, teaching, and preaching. Although his works do not quite equal his father's in sheer extent, they cover all the same fields.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01407
He was a kind and generous man. Sarkar Agha assures us that there was no one in Kerman who had not, at some time, benefited from his assistance or received some affectionate attention from him.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i

Yet agitation was stirred up against him—agitation which, beneath the cloak of pious religious pretexts, actually served very worldly interests. It was an artificial movement. If one questioned the people taking part in it, one discovered that they were unable to read Arabic, or even Persian, and knew absolutely nothing about the theological questions supposedly at issue. Their very ignorance left them all the freer to indulge in aggressive disturbances against the Shaykhis.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01409

Here Sarkar Agha takes the opportunity to sketch what we might call a study of the spiritual and psychological character of this "resentment." His account lends to the life of Mohammad-Khan Kermani the significance of an exemplary biography.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01410

Fundamentally, the Shaykhis had merely encountered, in modern times, the fate that true Shiites had always known. Their persecutors behaved no differently from the Umayyads and the Abbasids. Again and again, attempts had been made to appropriate Shiism and use it as the pretext for a political movement or revolution.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01411

Those Shiites who refused such compromises inevitably found themselves, to a greater or lesser degree, at odds with the legalistic form of religion that such political enterprises tended to promote. Under these circumstances, Shiism sometimes had to conceal itself even from those who claimed its name. That is why the holy Imams themselves recommended to their followers the "discipline of secrecy" (ketmân, taqîyeh).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01412

We shall see again later how dangerous it could be simply to appeal directly to the teaching and spiritual guidance of the Imams, without intermediaries—especially when doing so meant examining questions whose scope extended infinitely beyond matters of legal status. Too many established positions and interests were threatened for such an appeal not to cause alarm.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01413
That is why the Imams descended from the Prophet have always stood as a challenge to the ambitions of this world.

Sarkar Agha concludes: From Adam down to our own day, there have always been minorities of this kind and majorities of that kind, in every religion and at every period. It is a law of nature: whoever differs from others arouses fear, and people turn upon him relentlessly, even if he is the most peaceful and silent of men (pp. 67–69).

Overwhelmed by sadness, Hajj Mohammad-Khan decided to move with his family to Tehran. But at Baghin, five farsakhs—about thirty kilometers—from Kerman, a solemn delegation caught up with him. It included prominent citizens, several of the most eminent shaykhs, bearing the title Hojjat al-Islâm, and even the royal prince Roknod-dawleh, then governor of Kerman and Baluchistan.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01416
They came to offer their apologies and implore him to return to Kerman. Moved by these friendly appeals, the shaykh yielded.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01417

A period of calm followed. The governor kept strict watch over the ruffians, troublemakers, and agitators. Yet, as we know, a mere handful of such people is enough to cause disturbances while leaving those responsible almost impossible to identify. The difficulty was all the greater because the shaykh insisted that his many followers must never answer violence with violence.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01418
Finally, in 1323 AH, the shaykh chose to retire to Langar, some seven farsakhs south of Kerman. He died there the following year, on 20 Moharram 1324 AH (1906).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01419
Taken as a whole, his writings form an imposing body of work and mark an essential stage in the history of the Shaykhi school (II, pp. 306–398).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01420

These writings also cover the whole field of learning, giving pride of place in every discipline to the teachings handed down from the holy Imams. They comprise 204 titles (in fact more, for the reasons already explained). Sixty-five are works in Persian, and barely twenty have so far been printed.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01421

Among them, we should single out the Kitâb al-Mobîn (II, pp. 344–347), a major work that systematically arranges the Imams’ traditions (akhbâr) according to the different branches of knowledge (published 1305–1324 AH/1887–1906, two folio volumes of 617 and 634 pages); Wasîlat al-Najât (II, p. 334, in Persian), an original investigation and synthesis organized around the four arkân, or “pillars”; Hidâyat al-mostarshid (II, p. 335, in Persian), conceived along the same lines; Misbâh al-sâlikîn (II, p. 339, in Persian; its title might be rendered Lampas viatorum, “Lamp of the Wayfarers”), organized around the triad also familiar from Sufism: sharî'at, tarîqat, haqîqât (revealed religious law, the mystical path, and spiritual realization); and Sharh al-Hadîthayn (II, p. 311), a masterly exercise in ta'wîl, or interpretation of the inner meaning, devoted to two traditions concerning Fâtima’s preeminence on the Day of Resurrection (published in Bombay, 1312 AH, 152 pages).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01422

I would particularly like to mention the Yanâbî' al-Hikmat (“Sources of Theosophy and Philosophy”), a work that I know from personal study to be an invaluable summa, recently published in two volumes at Kerman (1965). For some fifteen years, moreover, the shaykh devoted an entire course of teaching to expanding upon this work. The collected lessons (dorûs) fill an unpublished Persian folio volume of some thousand pages. I hope to discuss it more fully elsewhere.

4. Shaykh Hâjj Zaynol-'Âbidîn-Khân Kermânî (1276/1859–1360/1942)
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01423

The biography of his father, written with filial devotion by Sarkâr Âghâ (pp. 32–56), gives us an unusually vivid picture of the life of a spiritual community’s leader in the distant Iranian province of Kerman during the first half of this century. Its account is firsthand: Sarkâr Âghâ shared with his father the same spiritual intimacy that we have already seen among their predecessors.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01424

Zaynol-'Âbidîn Khân, born on 7 Rajab 1276 AH (1859) and deceased on 5 Jomâdâ I 1360 AH (1942), was only twelve when his father, Hâjj Mohammad Karîm-Khân, died (1288 AH). His elder brother, Mohammad-Khân, who succeeded their father, took complete responsibility for his education and introduced him to the Islamic sciences. As we have already noted, a close friendship bound the brothers despite the difference in their ages. Zaynol-'Âbidîn accompanied his brother throughout his life and on his journeys.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01425

Indeed, in his final years, burdened by trials and sorrow, the elder brother liked to say, “The visits of Zaynol-'Âbidîn-Khân are the only sweetness I still taste in this world.” Zaynol-'Âbidîn, for his part, valued nothing more than the long hours they spent studying together in their library. Their collaboration produced, among other things, the collection known as the Kitâb al-Mobîn, mentioned above. Shaykh Zaynol-'Âbidîn had a highly individual way of working.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01426

When he spoke to his son about the difficulties he encountered, he offered remarkably perceptive observations on how an idea slowly takes shape before a discovery, and on how repeated attempts to put it into writing—even attempts that seem premature—can help bring the discovery about. His way of life reflected his character. Profoundly indifferent to prejudice and social convention, he regarded his entire person, like his predecessors, as devoted to the service of the holy Imams.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01427

Five days each week he taught the higher divine wisdom, hikmat ilâhîya. On Thursday and Friday evenings, however, he delivered a lengthy sermon at the mosque. He spent eight to ten hours a day reading and writing, yet always found time for anyone who came with a question. He was a refuge to all, and no turn of events disturbed his even temper.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01428

Journeys that interrupt a life of this kind could only be pilgrimages. The shaykh went once to Mecca (1305 AH/1888), three times to the Shiite holy places in Iraq, and four times to Mashhad in Iran, to the shrine of the Eighth Imam. Even while traveling, he went on working and writing.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01429

During his lifetime there were still occasional attempts to stir up trouble against the Shaykhis, but it became clear that, whenever the authorities had the resolve to remove two or three agitators, peace and order quickly returned. The last seven years of the shaykh’s long life were overshadowed by serious illness. He watched events in the world, and Iran’s predicament in particular, with a clear-eyed pessimism: “It is not within human power to put things right.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01430

“We must wait until people themselves become aware of their unbridled selfishness and their worship of this world, until they despair of it.” Until then, why be surprised “if even under the name of religious sciences ('olûm-e dînîya), people pursue nothing but worldly aims?” (p. 55). Shaykh Zaynol-'Âbidîn received numerous ijâzât, formal authorizations to transmit and teach. The most important came from his elder brother, Hâjj Mohammad-Khân.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01431

Another was granted by Sayyed Hosayn, author of the great Qur’anic Tafsîr (commentary), and son of Sayyed Ja'far Yazdî. Both belonged to the Shaykhi line of transmission (silsila shaykhîya), and we have already had occasion to emphasize the exemplary case of Sayyed Ja'far. The wording of this authorization is of interest, since it was itself derived from Hâjj Mohammad-Khân—who listed his own authorizations and teachers (mashâyekh) at the beginning of his Kitâb al-Mobîn—and leads back through an unbroken chain to the earliest Shiite masters.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01432

A third authorization, dated 19 Jomâdâ I 1311 AH (1893), is equally revealing of the care taken to establish a continuous chain of transmission back to the Imams. It was issued by Shaykh 'Alî Bahrânî, son of Shaykh Hasan, who had been among those who fled Bahrain for Iran and was a friend of Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01433

Shaykh 'Alî Bahrânî had himself received one authorization from Mohammad Karîm-Khân and another from Mollâ Hosayn Ganjavî. The latter’s authorization, received from Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, leads back link by link to Kolaynî (d. 329 AH/941), author of the Kitâb al-Kâfî, one of the foundational books of Shiism, and through him to the holy Imams. The writings left by Shaykh Zaynol-'Âbidîn-Khân form a body of work worthy of his predecessors (II, pp. 400–464).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01434

There are 153 titles, about half in Persian, of which scarcely more than twenty-five have appeared in print. In particular, almost all the treatises on hikmat ilâhîya, divine wisdom—many of which explore symbols of Shiite theosophy drawn from the Qur’an and the Imams’ traditions—remain unpublished. His series of lectures on the nature of prophecy, covering prophecy in general (nobowwat 'âmma) and the specific prophetic mission (nobowwat khâssa), survives in several substantial manuscripts. Yet even these represent only part of what he taught; his disciples unfortunately disposed of the rest.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i

5. Shaykh Abû'l-Qâsem-Khân Ebrâhîmî, Sarkâr Âghâ (1314/1896–1389/1969)
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01435

The fifth successor to Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î as head of the Shaykhi community was Shaykh Abû'l-Qâsem-Khân Ebrâhîmî, better known by his honorific title, “Sarkâr Âghâ.” Born in Kerman in 1314 AH/1896, he was the son of Shaykh Zaynol-'Âbidîn-Khân and the grandson of Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî. He died only recently, on 3 December 1969, in Mashhad, where he had gone on his annual pilgrimage.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01436

We had met him barely a month earlier, on 9 November, during his stay in Tehran, little knowing that this conversation would be our last. Having benefited over many years in Iran from his teaching on the matters discussed here, I recall him with the respect inspired by the memory of his spiritual strength and profound learning. His writings reflect many of the challenges he faced, challenges scarcely different from those now confronting his son and successor, Shaykh 'Abdol-Rezâ Khân.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01437

In a few pages of the major work to which we have been referring, a deep sadness breaks through. He wonders why, although “our mashâyekh [our shaykhs] have replied in hundreds of treatises, the same objections are endlessly repeated, and they still miss the point, for they never contain even the beginnings of an argument; they merely repeat suspicions, conjectures, accusations…” (p. 17).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01438

Three of Sarkâr Âghâ’s major works in Persian deserve particular attention here. a) Ijtihâd o taqlîd. — This substantial work raises such urgent questions that it calls for an extended analysis, which there is no room to undertake here. Its two title words can be understood only against the background of a controversy that has remained so fierce among Shiites that we must confine ourselves to a few cautious indications. It is the great dispute between the two schools known respectively as Osûlî and Akhbârî.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01439

Vital questions are at stake: nothing less than how the whole body of Shiite traditions is to be interpreted. The dispute is generally treated as a matter for jurists, chiefly concerning fiqh, or Islamic jurisprudence. Sarkâr Âghâ’s great achievement is to restore the question to its proper level and show that, beneath the choice between these two schools, the whole of theosophy—and with it the whole of Imami Shiism—is also at issue.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01440

The school of the Osûlîyûn, whom we may simply call the Osûlîs (from osûl, “foundations,” “principles,” or “general laws”), has become the larger school in numbers. Its adherents evaluate and interpret traditions from the Prophet and the Imams by applying rational principles and standards drawn from outside the traditions themselves; the traditions’ contents are then judged by those standards. This tendency probably first appeared in Shiism in a book by Abû Ja'far Tûsî (d. 460 AH/1067), who wished to demonstrate that Shiites were just as capable as Sunnis of using qiyâs—a word meaning both “analogy” and “syllogism”—even though the Imams had never accepted qiyâs, and Shiites could not recognize it as legitimate.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01441

All the more so because, in the Osûlî view, certainty cannot be reached about the divine intentions expressed in the Qur’an’s words, the exact meaning of those words, the authenticity of traditions (hadîth) attributed to the holy Imams, or even what those traditions were precisely intended to mean.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01442
In short, one can reach only an opinion, a conjectural form of knowledge (zann), and offer only a conjectural proof (borhân mazanna), as though by a kind of divination.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01443

We can now understand why ijtihâd, closed in Sunni Islam for centuries, has remained open in Shiism. Ijtihâd means the painstaking, persistent effort of study, sustained over many years, by which someone seeks to master the religious Law and become qualified to issue a theological judgment carrying authority. Those who attain this office or dignity through their studies are the Mojtaheds. Their standing is broadly comparable to that of the four “imams” associated with the Sunni schools of law—the Hanbalite, Hanafite, Malikite, and Shafiite schools.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01444

The philosophical assumption behind the Mojtaheds’ undertaking is that their rational intellect and reasoning ('aql) play a role equivalent to that of divine inspiration (ilhâm) in the Prophet (nabî) and the Imam. For the theosophers, by contrast, inspiration belongs to the holy intellect ('aql qodsî, intellectus sanctus), is fundamentally higher than ordinary reason, and can never be its equivalent.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01445

The path of ijtihâd is open to any Shiite with sufficient time and resources. In practice, however, only a small number become Mojtaheds. Because their learning and judgments carry authority, most believers follow their opinions, freely choosing the Mojtahed they prefer. To follow, or conform oneself to, the opinion of one’s chosen Mojtahed is taqlîd. The two words in the title of Sarkâr Âghâ’s book should now be clear.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01446

There is also the school of the Akhbârîyûn, whom again we may simply call the Akhbârîs. These are believers who accept the Qur’an, along with the entire corpus of hadîth and akhbâr in the Imami tradition, in its entirety and according to its literal wording. They can certainly claim a continuous Shiite tradition reaching back to the Imams, whereas the criteria used by the Osûlîs were codified comparatively recently (we shall return to this). Their leading figure in the Safavid period was Mohammad Amîn Astarâbâdî (d. 1033 AH/1623–1624).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01447

Yet because of their literalism, they are generally thought of as people of uncomplicated spirituality, uninvolved in theosophy or mysticism, in hikmat or 'irfân (philosophical wisdom or mystical knowledge). This is not entirely fair. As we have already noted, the Akhbârîs include distinguished theosophers such as Mohsen Fayz, pupil and son-in-law of Mollâ Sadrâ (d. around 1091 AH/1680). His book Safinat al-Najât, “The Ark of Salvation,” shows that he knew perfectly well that interpreting the problem went far beyond the strictly legal sphere.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01448

Another is Qazî Sa'îd Qommî, whom we have discussed at length above. We should also remember Mîrzâ Mohammad Neyshâpûrî Akhbârî (d. 1232 AH/1817), renowned for his knowledge of the occult sciences. The Shaykhis, then, reject the rationalism of the Osûlîs and stand much closer to the Akhbârîs.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01449

Yet the two must not be confused, any more than Shaykhi theosophy should be confused with that of Mollâ Sadrâ’s school, or Shaykhi mysticism with Sufism. The Shaykhis hold that conjectural knowledge is not enough: spiritual life is impossible without certainty. No legal ruling, no system of jurisprudence, can provide that certainty.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01450

The Qur’an and the traditions of the Prophet and the holy Imams are both necessary and sufficient. Just as there must be no intermediary between the Book of God and the believer, so there must be none between the Imams’ traditions and those who follow them. We have here something like a Shiite version of the Reformation principle Scriptura sacra sui ipsius interpres: Holy Scripture is its own interpreter.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01451

We must add, however, that in this case Scripture’s self-interpretation first takes shape in the tradition, that is, in the inspiration (ilhâm) of the holy Imams. This does away, by that very fact, with the Mojtaheds’ role as intermediaries—a consequence unlikely to have made life any easier for the Shaykhi school. For the only legitimate or conceivable taqlîd is thus a direct adherence to the holy Imams themselves. This immediate relationship also accords perfectly with the Imams’ injunction not to resort to qiyâs, reasoning by analogy.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01452

The task is to bring their traditions to bear on each individual case, discovering each time which tradition, or traditions, apply. Once again, the movement of thought is not dialectical but essentially interpretive—an exercise in ta'wîl, the search for inner meaning. The most fervent traditionalism thus proves capable of generating perpetual renewal: a new meaning may emerge every day. One must seek it out, and that is the very fruitfulness of esoteric knowledge.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01453

Someone will no doubt ask: how, then, can the authenticity of these hadîth and akhbâr be judged? How can we know whether the Imams really said this or that? We shall return to this question. Put in those terms, it is the characteristic question of the historian who approaches the texts from the outside, a question that such a historian can hardly avoid asking.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01454

But a phenomenologist, attending to religious experience as it is lived, discerns another question: where is the “place” from which the Imam speaks, and in which his words carry authority? The Imams are no longer physically present in this world. Their authority, which allows no intermediary, must therefore be inward. The “place” where it operates—and where the Imams’ words are heard, and were heard in earlier times—is Shiite consciousness itself. Without that consciousness, no one would even have cared to transmit the texts to us.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01455

Is it not possible that, in the intensity of meditation, as the Imam’s presence becomes real to consciousness, his voice may be heard in words that take the form, on the lips or under the pen of the transmitter, of a sermon (khotba) or a narrative such as the story of the White Cloud? At that moment, we would say, whatever the name of the “secretary” (amanuensis) holding the pen, it is the Imam who speaks. (For this reason, the only adequate textual inquiry would be one concerned with the history of literary forms, or Formgeschichte.) Without this phenomenological understanding, we shall never understand the religious phenomenon of Shiism—or, indeed, religious experience as such.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01456

Any criticism imposed entirely from outside, seeking to subject that experience to the laws of the external world, only breaks it apart. This has been our approach to interpretation throughout the present work. For the Imam’s real existence, his spiritual existence, is something other than the outward record of deeds accessible to external history. Nor is that real existence confined to the period of his visible appearance in history: if it were, there could be neither Shiite religion nor Shiite consciousness.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01457

Shiite consciousness—the malakût, or spiritual realm, of the Shiite believer—is the only place where the Imam speaks and speaks with authority (recall the tradition of the White Cloud). The Imam is himself the history, the true history, of Shiite consciousness: a spiritual history whose events are inward visions. These observations should convey the weight of what is at stake in Sarkâr Âghâ’s major work and explain its exceptional interest. The questions it addresses reach far beyond jurisprudence into the realm of faith and religious experience itself—the res religiosa.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01458

We can illustrate this here with only one example. A frequently debated question is whether a believer may, at least in matters of practical conduct, continue to follow a Mojtahed who has died, or whether that allegiance must be transferred to another. The usual answer is that it must be transferred to a living Mojtahed. The Shaykhis, however, make the following point.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01459

Taqlîd, in the ordinary sense of the word and in the all-too-common way it is practiced, amounts to simply agreeing—to accepting a Mojtahed’s “authority” without any further personal grounds. Instead of truly conforming oneself to a teaching, one is merely conforming to others. Whether the Mojtahed is living or dead makes no difference: the practice becomes, quite simply, the same as that of the Sunnis.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01460

But if we attend to the spiritual, true meaning of the conduct designated by taqlîd, we must recognize that it can only mean “conforming oneself” to the teaching of the Imams (as a tradition of the Seventh Imam, Mûsâ Kâzem, makes clear). Any taqlîd centered on the Mojtahed as a person has no foundation.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01461

A Mojtahed cannot be said to speak by virtue of a rule-making authority vested in him personally. He interprets; he explains matters to those who have lacked the time or ability to “search” for themselves; he helps each person make the teaching his or her own (tashkhîs, an individual act of discernment and appropriation). The only voice that speaks with authority is that of the Imam himself, through a khabar, a transmitted teaching that brings out the hidden meaning of the revealed Book.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01462

In that sense, a fatwâ, or legal opinion, is not different in kind from a khabar: it translates, develops, and deepens it. The value of a scholar who possesses this gift of interpretation therefore endures whether he is alive or dead, just as the content of a khabar endures whether its transmitter (râwî) is living or dead.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01463

If the Shaykhis acknowledge such spiritual authority in their three great shaykhs, they do so because those teachers remained faithful in their interpretation and explanation of the Prophet’s and the Imams’ teachings. That is the sole reason. What may appear from the outside as an “innovation,” as the teaching passes from one shaykh to another, is in reality no more than the lifting of the veil of taqîyeh—the precautionary concealment of belief—on a point that might previously have required it.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01464

Every Shiite, moreover, has a calling to ijtihâd, provided he possesses the necessary learning together with the moral and spiritual qualifications. The insistence on both conditions means that the very idea of “legal specialization” developing independently of the spiritual demands of religious life can only be a distortion. Likewise, because the Imam alone possesses authority, no “clergy” can claim it for themselves.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01465

Finally, in practice, all Shiites, Mojtaheds or not, take the “Hidden Imam” as their guide in taqlîd, following the final instruction left to his last nâ'ib, or representative (329 AH/940). Since the Hidden Imam is alive and invisibly present, the question of giving one’s allegiance to a dead man cannot arise.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01466
Yet that, in Shiite eyes, is unfortunately what Sunni scholars have done, piling book upon book on the writings of their four “imams,” who truly are dead (pp. 10–14).
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01467

b) Risâla-ye Tanzîh al-Awliyâ. — This substantial work is chiefly a commentary on the Irshâd al-awâmm, itself written in Persian by Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî (mentioned above, § 2, p. 242). It answers sixty questions posed by various individuals about difficulties they encountered in reading that work, and consequently treats numerous essential points of 'irfân, or mystical theosophy.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01468

Here, however, we shall consider only one question of immediate relevance, a concern also visible in the first volume of the Fihrist (pp. 26 ff.): the unity, or reunification, of Islam and Muslims. In other words, the issue is certain contemporary attempts at a kind of “ecumenism” intended to bring together the Sunni majority and the Shiite minority.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01469

Clearly, the question takes on an entirely different meaning depending on whether one understands Shiism simply as a legal tradition or experiences it as the authentic form of spiritual Islam. In the first case, it is enough to “unite” Shiism with the four existing Sunni schools as a fifth school of law.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01470

In the second, for anyone who professes Shiism in its fullness, the walâyat—the spiritual guardianship and guidance—of the Twelve Imams is the “inner meaning of prophecy.” It is therefore implied, together with the Prophet’s mission (risâlat), in the very words of the profession of faith, the shahâdat. Their initiatory role in revealing the hidden, inward meaning of divine revelations makes them Guides upon the Way. At a higher level, they are ultimately understood to be the Way itself, and the meaning of that Way.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01471

A Shiite who knows the level of reality from which his personal, inward obligation of fidelity to the Imams arises cannot help seeing such efforts at “reunion” as concealing worldly motives and political ideologies, pushing toward compromises he cannot contemplate. We have already seen how rigorously Shaykhi thought condemns this sort of confusion. Once we grasp what faith and trust in the “Hidden Imam,” whose invisible presence sustains Shiite life, truly mean, two characteristic attitudes become easy to understand.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01472
First, the spirit of proselytism—missionary work or propaganda—is alien to this faith, for the invisible Imam alone can lead each consciousness inwardly to find the Way.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01473
Second, these efforts at reconciliation appear to a Shiite to debase and endanger the very thing they claim to save, without even understanding what it is.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01474

c) Risâla-ye falsafîya. — This final book is no less relevant to our own time than the preceding two. It answers twenty-five questions put to Sarkâr Âghâ by Mollâ Falsafî (8 Rabî' II 1369 lunar AH = 27 Bahman 1328 solar AH = 17 February 1950). The questions are searching, for they concern all the essential points of the four rokn (“pillars” or articles) that distinguish Shaykhi doctrine within Shiism.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01475

The replies are equally pointed and define the positions of the two sides with some spirit. In truth, the questionnaire was not without a conciliatory intention. Mollâ Falsafî hoped that the answers, once submitted for consideration to the great Mojtahed of Qomm, might make it possible to stop using the name “Shaykhis,” thus removing every suggestion or suspicion of “dissent.”
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01476
But as we have seen, the Shaykhis are not at all troubled by the name given to them; and when one professes their fidelity to the holy Imams, it would be difficult to feel oneself a “dissenter.”
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01477

In short, the questions and answers were published, and matters went no further. From this necessarily brief sketch of the Shaykhi school’s history and literary productivity, two things emerge. We encounter a doctrine and a form of religious experience characteristic of Shiite consciousness in our own time; and we encounter an entire library hitherto unknown in the West.
II. The Successors of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i
passage-en-01478

Adding up the material examined above gives us about a thousand titles, in Arabic and Persian—and actually more if we take account of the way the majmû'a, or collected volumes, are put together. Barely more than a quarter of these works have been published, and for several reasons the rest can only appear gradually.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01479

1. Tradition and Renewal
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01480

In these pages it is impossible to offer a detailed synthesis of Shaykhi doctrine, whose broad purpose embraces both a speculative understanding of the Imams and the spiritual regeneration of the believer. At the outset we recalled the Shiite tradition that Shaykhism was in fact bringing back to life, together with its representatives—not only in Safavid and pre-Safavid times but much further back, among those who surrounded the Imams themselves. It would be fruitless to judge this movement, or claim to “explain” it, from outside.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01481

As we have also noted, its purpose has often been confused with that of schools from which it is in fact clearly distinct. Tonkâbûnî, for example, describes the undertaking of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î—whom he acknowledges as an outstanding figure (sar-âmad)—as a synthesis of Shiite theology and philosophy, specifically the philosophy of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01482

But such a synthesis had been accomplished long before, from Haydar Âmolî and Ibn Abî Jomhûr down to Mollâ Sadrâ himself. And although Shaykh Ahmad wrote systematic commentaries on two of Mollâ Sadrâ’s works, he did not do so simply to adopt the philosophy of the master of Shiraz. He had something quite different in mind.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01483

Tonkâbûnî’s description would therefore make sense only if it pointed us toward a different kind of parallel: for example, the work of the great Ismaili thinkers Hamîdoddîn Kermânî and Nâsir-e Khosraw, especially the latter’s Jâmî' al-Hikmatayn, which seeks to bring together the two philosophies, Ismaili and Greek.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01484
Yet their work would probably have provoked among philosophers who were strictly Avicennian a reaction much like that of the nineteenth-century philosopher Hâdî Sabzavârî toward Shaykh Ahmad.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01485

What these two major forms of Shiite theosophy—Twelver and Ismaili—share is the very idea on which Shiism as a religious phenomenon rests: walâyat, the spiritual guardianship of the Imams, as the necessary counterpart of nobowwat, or prophetic mission. They share the conviction that the Qur’anic revelation, like every prophetic revelation, has both zâhir and bâtin: an outward meaning and an inward one; and that the role of the Imamate, and of the Imams’ teaching, is to guide people toward that inner meaning and initiate them into it.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01486

Walâyat and nobowwat are joined in the person of the Prophet, but the prophetic mission as such is to reveal the outward meaning, whereas walâyat is concerned with teaching the inward meaning. The cycle of prophecy ends with the last Prophet; the cycle of walâyat begins with the first Imam. It is this teaching that is meant when we refer to the immense body of traditions (akhbâr) transmitted from the Imams.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01487

But these traditions are not, in turn, literal commentaries on the Book and the Prophet’s hadîth. More often than not—especially where they concern the creation of the cosmos, the eternal preexistence of the fullness of the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones,” or the events of the last things—they speak in symbols.
III. Some Points of Doctrine
passage-en-01488

Some are as long as an entire lesson. They invite ta'wîl, interpretation that reveals their inner meaning, and other hadîth and akhbâr teach how to undertake that very interpretation. In our discussion of ijtihâd and taqlîd above, we saw how and why Shaykhi interpretation could preserve the whole body of traditions from the Imams.
